title: Actor Laith Nakli Faces Deportation Fight as His Biggest Film Opens
excerpt: The 56-year-old Manhattan actor's immigration case, closed in 2013, was reopened this year — one of nearly 150,000 sent back to court since January 2025 — as his film with Mahershala Ali wins critical attention.
body:
• Laith Nakli, 56, a Manhattan actor born in the United Kingdom to Syrian parents, is starring opposite Mahershala Ali in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother — and fighting a reopened deportation case at the same time, CNN reported.
  • His case was administratively closed in 2013 and reopened this year — one of nearly 150,000 cases the Trump administration has sent back to court since January 2025.
  • The case traces to a 2000 guilty plea to four counts of conspiracy to possess and distribute controlled substances — illegal steroids — for which he received three years' probation, community service and a $3,000 fine.
  • For readers in similar positions: a closed case is not a decided case. Nakli appeared in immigration court on October 30, and his next hearing is about a month away.

Laith Nakli will not be at the Hollywood premiere of the biggest film of his career. He has seen the reports of immigration officers detaining people at airports, CNN reported, and flying to California feels too risky. On screen he acts alongside Oscar winner Mahershala Ali in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother. Off screen, he is preparing for a court date that could end with his deportation from the country where, as he puts it in a sworn declaration, his life, his family and his future are.

"It's a crazy fear that you live in. In today's age, anything can happen."

— Laith Nakli, to CNN

How a closed case came back

Nakli was born to Syrian parents in the United Kingdom and holds citizenship in both countries. In 2000 he pleaded guilty to four counts of conspiracy to possess and distribute controlled substances — in his case, illegal steroids from his bodybuilding years. The charges carried a maximum sentence of 20 years. US District Judge Frederic Block sentenced him instead to three years' probation, community service and a $3,000 fine.

The plea followed him into immigration court. In 2011, the Department of Homeland Security accused Nakli of fraud, alleging he had not acknowledged the arrest in immigration paperwork, and cited the drug charges as crimes of moral turpitude. In 2013 the government stopped its efforts and the case was administratively closed. Administrative closure is not a ruling in the immigrant's favour — it shelves a case. This year the administration reopened his, one of nearly 150,000 cases sent back to court since January 2025 as part of its immigration crackdown, according to CNN.

The legal fight now running on two tracks

Nakli's attorneys have petitioned in federal court to vacate the 2000 conviction, arguing his lawyer at the time did not advise him that the plea could carry serious immigration consequences. "Had I known this plea carried mandatory deportation regardless of the sentence, I would never have accepted it," he wrote in a sworn declaration, as reported by SSBCrack's account of the CNN reporting. Judge Block has denied that petition, and a motion asking him to reconsider is pending. In parallel, the immigration case itself is live: Nakli appeared at a hearing at 26 Federal Plaza in New York on October 30, his first since 2013, and the next hearing is about a month away. A Homeland Security spokesperson offered no specific reason for reopening his case, saying his claims will be heard by an immigration judge.

What to watch

Two decisions decide Nakli's future. If the federal court reconsiders and vacates the 2000 conviction, the foundation of the deportation case weakens sharply. If it does not, an immigration judge will decide whether a plea taken 26 years ago — followed by an acting career and no accusation of a new crime in the record CNN reviewed — ends his life in the United States. Either way, his case is a working demonstration of the mechanism now reaching tens of thousands of people whose files were closed years ago: closure was a pause, not an ending.
